>Ane, this whole repository is built on top of your work. The code you sent me already had every load-bearing physical insight — the patched solver, the aperture filter, the dispersion model, the surface profile, the polarisation averaging, the comparison protocol against FTIR triples. What I did was *re-house* it so it could be swept systematically, *quantify* what counts as a good fit, and *characterise* the boundary where the model stops being trustworthy. That boundary turned out to coincide exactly with where your AJUSTE PDF reports its results — at $\theta$ = 30° — and the parameter configuration my sweep landed on is the parameter configuration you committed to empirically.
>
>If you find the rest of this useful, the next move I would suggest is parked research item $\gamma$′ — the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ phonon-aware $k(\lambda)$ — because that is the single largest residual driver and the one improvement that would let Stage 2 and Stage 3 land at meaningful values rather than fitting around oxide error. Anything else here, ask me.
>
>— Josu 


## What this document is, and how to read it

This is a **chronological tour** of everything I have done with the files you sent me on 8 May 2026. The structure of the repository looks larger than it really is, so the goal here is to *flatten* it into one story you can read in one sitting.

Read it linearly the first time — every section refers forward to the next one. On the second pass you can jump to any phase from the table of contents below.

**Three things to keep in mind while you read:**

1. **Everything you sent me is preserved untouched.** Your `.ipynb` files, the CSVs, the paper, the patched `solver.py` / `harmonics.py` — they all live verbatim in [`20260508_messages/`](20260508_messages/) and [`ane_originals/`](ane_originals/). Nothing of yours was modified. The "active" code in [`simulation/`](simulation/) is a *parallel* reorganised version that calls into the same physics.

2. **I did not change any physics that you wrote.** The RCWA solve cell in [`simulation/lib/sweep_runner.py`](simulation/lib/sweep_runner.py) is a line-by-line port of your `test8.qmd §5`. The differences are *structural* (turning your cell into a function, persisting outputs, parameterising inputs), not physical.

3. **The big result is at the end** — see §10. To save you scrolling: at **$\theta$ = 30° on sample SS_12-3** the simulation reproduces your experimental FTIR with **Pearson r $\geq$ 0.95** across all five azimuths, and the parameter configuration that achieves this **matches your empirical fit exactly** ($t_{\text{oxide}}$ = 0.9 µm, $\beta$ = 2°, HS_caliente — see page 10 of your AJUSTE PDF). Outside $\theta$ $\leq$ 30° the model has a clear physics limitation that I have characterised but not solved — see §9.

## 1. The starting point — what you sent me on 2026-05-08

You sent me five things by email on 8 May, which are archived verbatim in [`20260508_messages/`](20260508_messages/):

| File | What it is | Role |
|---|---|---|
| [`Test8_full (1).ipynb`](20260508_messages/Test8_full%20(1).ipynb) | Your "Programa principal" — the full simulation pipeline | The thing whose results we wanted to reproduce and extend |
| [`Representacion.ipynb`](20260508_messages/Representacion.ipynb) | Your plotting / comparison helpers | Shows how you compared simulation against experimental FTIR |
| [`SS_letter (1).csv`](20260508_messages/SS_letter%20(1).csv) | Stainless-steel complex permittivity $\varepsilon$($\tilde{\nu}$), 400–7000 cm⁻¹ | Substrate material data |
| [`calientes_cromo.csv`](20260508_messages/calientes_cromo.csv) | Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ (n, k) for **HS** films (substrate heated to 300 °C) | Oxide overlayer for "hot" films |
| [`indices_cromo.csv`](20260508_messages/indices_cromo.csv) | Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ (n, k) for **RS** films (unheated substrate) | Oxide overlayer for "cold" films |
| [`paper_datos_cromo.pdf`](20260508_messages/paper_datos_cromo.pdf) | Al-Kuhaili & Durrani, *Optical Materials* 29 (2007) 709–713 | Source of the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ dispersion model |

And two **patched Python files** (inlined into your email, not standalone): `solver.py` and `harmonics.py`, modifications of the upstream [`rcwa`](https://rcwa.readthedocs.io) package adding two things:

1. **Exit-angle tracking** — `Solver.theta_orders`, the polar angle of every diffraction order *m* given the current source and grating.
2. **A detected-reflectance aperture filter** — `Solver.get_detected_reflectance(beta_deg)`, which sums `R_m` only over the orders that fall inside $\pm\beta$/2 of the specular direction.

That second feature turned out to be load-bearing for everything that followed — see §3 below.

I also have your two PDFs in [`ane_originals/`](ane_originals/): **AJUSTE DE PARÁMETROS — PROGRAMA EDMUNDS** and **Tratamiento de imágenes. Modelos y comparación con medidas experimentales**. Reading those carefully is what allowed me to recognise, at the end of the run, that my best-fit parameters and yours were the same parameters.

## 2. Phase 1 — Cold reading and analysis (2026-05-08)

### The document
[`ANALYSIS.md`](ANALYSIS.md) — long, detailed, written before I touched a single line of your code.

### Why I wrote it first
Before reorganising anything or running anything, I wanted to *understand what your code was actually computing* and to flag every place where the physics or the code looked fragile. If I jumped straight into a parameter sweep without that, I would have spent days fitting around an unknown.

### What's in it
A file-by-file inventory, the physics chain in one diagram, the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ optical model laid out from the paper, and **10 catalogued issues** with severity tags (HIGH / MED / LOW). Worth your attention in particular:

| Severity | Issue | Section |
|---|---|---|
| **HIGH (physics)** | The Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ $k(\lambda)$ model is the Al-Kuhaili sub-bandgap tail fitted on **0.3–2.5 µm transmittance**. You and I use it on **3–25 µm** — that's a 10× extrapolation outside the fit range, and the model contains **zero phonon physics**. This was the single most-likely structural error, and §10 confirms it turned out to be load-bearing. | [`ANALYSIS.md §4`](ANALYSIS.md), §6.3 |
| **MED (physics)** | The header of `SS_letter (1).csv` says `wavenumber, n, k` but the values are actually `wavenumber, ε', ε''` (real and imaginary permittivity, not refractive index). Your code uses them correctly **as** permittivity, so the science is right — the header just lies. | [`ANALYSIS.md §5`](ANALYSIS.md) |
| **MED (physics)** | The oxide is applied as a *vertical band* above the local metal column, not normal-to-the-surface. On a sinusoid with depth 3 µm and period 13 µm the surface slope reaches $\approx$ 36°; a real oxide grown perpendicular to the surface has up to 25 % more vertical extent on the slopes. Effect is $\approx$ proportional to oxide thickness. | [`ANALYSIS.md §6.4`](ANALYSIS.md) |
| **MED (modelling)** | The substrate stack is `air | grating | 200 µm SS | air` — not a true semi-infinite SS. **Important update from §8 below: I tested this empirically and at our wavelengths it is bit-identical to the semi-infinite version.** The 200 µm slab is already > 1000× the IR skin depth, so light decays before reaching the back. The geometric concern was valid, the physical impact is zero. | [`ANALYSIS.md §6.7`](ANALYSIS.md) |
| **HIGH (portability)** | Hard-coded Windows paths and a leaky-closure bug in `Representacion.ipynb`'s `get_una` / `get_prom`: functions take `(periodo, profundidad, …)` but the body uses module-level `period` and `prof` from the surrounding cell. Works as long as the outer cell defines them; silently wrong otherwise. | [`ANALYSIS.md §6.8`](ANALYSIS.md) |
| LOW | `'./SS_letter.csv'` ≠ `'SS_letter (1).csv'` — the notebook will not run on a fresh checkout. | [`ANALYSIS.md §6.1`](ANALYSIS.md) |
| LOW | `_check_converged` raises `RuntimeError('… {self.max_iters} …')` — missing the `f`-string prefix. | [`ANALYSIS.md §6.9`](ANALYSIS.md) |

### One sanity-check I did before doing anything else
I smoke-tested the `rcwa 1.0.48` install (Python 3.12 venv) against the analytic Fresnel result for vacuum / n = 3 at normal incidence: `R = 0.250000, T = 0.750000, R + T = 1.000000` — exact. So the runtime is fine. Every issue in `ANALYSIS.md` is about *your set-up*, not about the package.

### One subtlety from §7 worth flagging
The paper's claim "n_HS > n_RS" is true near the absorption edge — that's the regime the paper actually fitted. In our IR regime, the *empirical sub-bandgap tail* of the model gives **k_RS > k_HS**, which is **the opposite trend**. Real Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ in the mid-IR is dominated by **phonons** that the empirical tail does not contain, so this reversal is an artefact of the extrapolation, not a measured property. I flag it here because, if ever you compare HS vs RS at long $\lambda$, the relative ordering you see is the parametrised tail, not real material physics. (See §10 — this turned out to matter.)

## 3. Phase 2 — Decoupled comparison and the distance metric (2026-05-08)

### Why this came next
We needed **one number per simulation run** — small if the simulation matches your experimental FTIR, large if it does not. Without that scalar, no sweep can have an objective; we would just be staring at curves.

### What I built
- A **read-only snapshot** of your 321 experimental FTIR CSV files, copied into [`data/experimental/`](data/experimental/) and marked `a-w`. The source folder you flagged as off-limits stays untouched.
- [`simulation/exploratory/compare.qmd`](simulation/exploratory/compare.qmd): a Quarto document that, for one simulation configuration, overlays the simulated `R(λ)` and `R_det(β)` curves on the mean of the experimental triple, plots the residual, and computes the scalar distance.
- [`simulation/design/DISTANCE.md`](simulation/design/DISTANCE.md): the formal definition of the distance metric, the motivation behind every choice, and the configuration-space architecture that follows from it.

### The distance metric, in one box

$$
\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}
= \frac{1}{N - k}\,
\sum_{i=1}^{N}
\left(
\frac{R_{\text{sim}}(\lambda_i) - \langle R_{\text{exp}}(\lambda_i)\rangle}
     {\max\!\bigl(\sigma_{\bar R}(\lambda_i),\, \sigma_{\text{floor}}\bigr)}
\right)^{2}
$$

with $\sigma_{\bar R}$ the standard error of the mean across your 3 FTIR repeats, $\sigma_{\text{floor}} = 0.01$ (1 % absolute), $k$ the number of free parameters in the current optimisation, and $N$ the number of wavelength points in the overlap of the simulation grid and the experimental grid.

This is just reduced chi-squared with a sensible noise floor. The two nuances:

- **Divide by SEM, not std.** That gives $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ $\approx$ 1 a physical meaning: "the simulation sits within experimental scatter, on average".
- **Floor at 1 %.** With only 3 repeats, sample std collapses at bins where the repeats happen to coincide. The floor encodes the prior that no FTIR bin is intrinsically more precise than ~1 % absolute reflectance.

### The very first comparison run — and why it changed everything

I ran your `test8` defaults (`t_oxide = 0.9 µm`, NA = 35, $\theta$ = 30°, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89°) once and computed two scalars: one comparing **$R_{\text{total}}$** (sum over all propagating diffraction orders) against your FTIR triple `12-3_30_0_*.CSV`, and one comparing **$R_{\text{det}}(\beta = 2^{\circ})$** (your patched aperture filter, summing only orders within $\pm$1° of specular):

| Metric | $R_{\text{total}}$ | $R_{\text{det}}$ $\beta$ = 2° |
|---|---:|---:|
| $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ | 749 | **137** |
| RMSE | 0.274 | **0.117** |
| MAE | 0.228 | **0.108** |
| max \|residual\| | 0.553 | **0.244** |
| Pearson r | **0.83** | **0.97** |

`R_det(β = 2°)` crushes `R_total` on every metric. The Pearson correlation jumps from 0.83 to **0.97** — meaning the *shape* of your simulated curve already tracks the experiment closely; the disagreement is almost entirely a uniform amplitude offset.

**Conclusion that fell out immediately:** the FTIR detector is **aperture-limited**, not hemispherical. The 6 percentage-point uniform offset between $\langle R_{\det} \rangle \approx 0.60$ and $\langle R_{\exp} \rangle \approx 0.54$ is exactly the residual we want the sweep to close. Which means **the right observable to compare against the experiment is `R_det(β)`, with $\beta$ found by the sweep, never `R_total`.**

This is the single most important piece of advice I would offer for any future FTIR comparison: pick a $\beta$, sweep over it, never default to `R_total`.

## 4. Phase 3 — Configuration-space framework (2026-05-08)

### Why this came next
Knowing we needed to minimise $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ doesn't tell us *which parameters to vary*. A naïve Cartesian sweep over every plausible knob is intractable. We need a principled tiering.

### What I built
[`simulation/design/DISTANCE.md`](simulation/design/DISTANCE.md) (long document — sections 4 and 6 are the load-bearing ones), and the SS_12-3- specific sweep plan [`simulation/design/SWEEP_PLAN.md`](simulation/design/SWEEP_PLAN.md).

### The four-tier inclusion rule
A configuration-space dimension only earns its slot if it is **(i) genuinely uncertain**, **(ii) measurably affects the simulation output**, and **(iii) physically meaningful** — i.e. learning its best value teaches us something. By that test:

- **Tier 1 — must sweep.** `t_oxide` (your oxide thickness was a placeholder), `β` (detector aperture, the dominant residual driver per §3), `oxide_dispersion` (categorical: HS / RS / [phonon-aware model when we have one]).
- **Tier 2 — sweep with tight priors.** `period_um` (your AFM gives 12.85 $\pm$ 0.05 µm), `depth_um` (AFM gives 2.40 µm, sinusoid amplitude fit gives 2.52 µm — wider prior).
- **Tier 3 — set, don't sweep.** `harmonics` (a convergence parameter, not a fit parameter), `slices`, `theta`/`phi_exp` (these are the *conditions* under which we evaluate the simulation, not knobs), `phi_sim − phi_exp` convention (a discrete coordinate choice, fix after one sanity check), `ur` (truly fixed for non-magnetic materials).
- **Tier 4 — exclude.** An overall `R_scale` calibration factor would absorb the very offsets we want to *identify*; introducing it now would hide which Tier-1 knob is the real culprit.

### Universal vs per-sample
Crucially, some parameters should be *the same across all six samples* (instrument + material constants — $\beta$, oxide dispersion, possibly $t_{\text{oxide}}$) and some are *per-sample* (period and depth from the AFM of each plate). The sweep architecture is therefore hierarchical:

- **Outer loop** — universal Tier-1 parameters.
- **Inner loop** — per-sample Tier-2 geometry, refit per sample under the locked universal parameters.

### The staged sweep
Naïvely the cost is multiplicative (6 samples × 15 ($\theta$, $\varphi$) × universal cube) and runs to weeks. Factored by stage, the cost becomes tractable:

| Stage | Goal | What varies | Conditions | Runs |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **0a** convergence | Smallest NA at which $R_{\text{det}}$ is stable | `harmonics` | one ($\theta$, $\varphi$) | 8 |
| **0b** $\varphi$ convention | Confirm $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ ↔ $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ mapping | `phi_sim` | one ($\theta$, $\varphi$) | 4 |
| **1** universal Tier-1 | Best ($t_{\text{oxide}}$, $\beta$, oxide_dispersion) | Tier 1 | one ($\theta$, $\varphi$), one sample | 84 |
| **2** per-sample geometry | Best (period, depth) for SS_12-3 | Tier 2 | all 15 ($\theta$, $\varphi$) | 375 |
| **3** generalisation | Validate Tier-1 across the other 5 samples | Tier 2, per sample | all 15 ($\theta$, $\varphi$) × 5 | 1875 |

With decision points between stages. The single non-negotiable one: **after Stage 1, if best $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ $\gg$ 1, do not proceed to Stage 2** — the bottleneck is structural and Stage 2 would absorb model error into geometry parameters. (Spoiler: it did, and we did not proceed.)

This staging is what made the campaign finishable in a long weekend rather than a month.

## 5. Phase 4 — Building the orchestration code (2026-05-09)

### Why this came next
At this point we had a metric, a tiering, and a plan. What was still missing was *runnable infrastructure*: a way to take a parameter dict, solve one RCWA configuration, score it against the experiment, and persist the result — without copy-pasting your notebook cells across stages.

### What I built
One module, [`simulation/lib/sweep_runner.py`](simulation/lib/sweep_runner.py) (~390 lines), exposing essentially four functions:

```python
solve_one(cfg: SimConfig)                      # one RCWA solve, both polarisations
average_polarisations(...)                     # (R_LX + R_LY) / 2
load_experimental_repeats(sample, θ, φ_exp)    # mean + SEM across the 3 FTIR CSVs
score(sim_df, sample, …)                       # χ²_red, RMSE, MAE, Pearson, … for R and R_det
run_one_config(cfg, …)                         # solve + score + persist + return one row
```

`SimConfig` is a frozen dataclass that names every parameter the simulation needs (period, A, $t_{\text{oxide}}$, oxide_dispersion, $\theta$, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$, harmonics, slices, $\beta$, $A_2$, $\varphi_2$, semi_infinite_substrate, wavelengths). The filename stem is derived from the config, so every run is uniquely identified on disk — this matters because the sweep is restartable.

**The physics inside `solve_one()` is your `test8.qmd §5` cell, line by line.** I moved it into a function and removed the magic-number defaults, but `discretize_with_oxide`, the `LayerStack` construction, the `Source` parameters, and the `Solver.solve()` call are unchanged. Where the active code diverges from yours, it is structural (function, not script; parameterised, not hard-coded; persisted, not transient). The numbers should be identical to your `test8` for matching parameters; I verified this in the smoke test.

### Two paradigms, one project
- **Scripts run, reports consume.** Heavy execution lives in [`simulation/sweep/bin/run_*.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/) — pure Python, parallelisable (multiprocessing with `--parallel N`), restartable via `--resume`. Each script writes a `results.csv` and a `traces/` directory of per-config `AVG_*.csv` files.
- **Reports** in [`simulation/sweep/reports/`](simulation/sweep/reports/) are Quarto documents that load the scripts' `results.csv` and render the analysis. They never call RCWA themselves — render time is seconds, not hours.
- **Exploratory single-config work** lives in [`simulation/exploratory/`](simulation/exploratory/) — Quarto documents for iterating on *one* configuration interactively ([`simulate.qmd`](simulation/exploratory/simulate.qmd) is the parameterised successor to your `test8.qmd`; [`compare.qmd`](simulation/exploratory/compare.qmd) is the comparison document from §3).

### Where your code lives now
- Your two patched files (`solver.py`, `harmonics.py`) need to be on `sys.path` before the `rcwa` import — easiest is to drop them into the venv's `rcwa/` site-packages once, which is what the venv at `.venv/` has done.
- Your original notebooks are in [`20260508_messages/`](20260508_messages/) verbatim, and as `.qmd` conversions in [`ane_originals/`](ane_originals/) for legibility. None of those is on the active execution path.

## 6. Phase 5 — The staged sweep, run by run

Everything below was run on this MacBook, Python 3.12, `rcwa 1.0.48` in [`.venv/`](.venv/), on 2026-05-09. The wall times include I/O. Every run's command, wall time, parameters, and key numbers are recorded in [`RUN_LOG.md`](RUN_LOG.md) — what follows is the narrative.

### 6.1 Stage 0a — Harmonics-count convergence

**The question.** What is the smallest harmonics count NA such that `R_det(λ; NA)` is stable across the full 3–25 µm band to better than the 1 % $\sigma$-floor? Without this answer, every other axis of the sweep would be fitting around a numerical artefact.

**Setup.** Centre of the cube ($t_{\text{oxide}}$ = 0.30 µm placeholder, $\beta$ = 2°, HS_caliente, $\theta$ = 30°, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89°). Eight NA values: 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 39, 51.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage0a.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage0a.py) — 8 configs, 4 workers, **17.1 min wall**.

**Result.**

| NA | max\|$R_{\text{det}}$(NA) − $R_{\text{det}}$(51)\| |
|---:|---:|
| 15 | 0.1750 |
| 19 | 0.1168 |
| 23 | 0.0749 |
| 27 | 0.0462 |
| 31 | 0.0267 |
| 35 | 0.0136 |
| **39** | **0.0063** ← chosen |
| 51 | 0.0000 (reference) |

**Decision.** **NA = 39.** Smallest grid value where the band-max disagreement with NA = 51 is below the 1 % $\sigma$-floor. Locked for every subsequent stage.

**Aside.** Your note in the original notebook said *"a partir de 27; pero mejor usar 31"* — that was for the broad-cone problem; once we restrict to $R_{\text{det}}(\beta = 2^{\circ})$ the cone is narrow enough that NA = 31 still leaves a 2.7 % residual at long $\lambda$, and NA = 39 is needed to get under 1 %. Your eye was right; the floor was just slightly tighter than your visual criterion.

The detailed report: [`simulation/sweep/reports/stage0a_report.qmd`](simulation/sweep/reports/stage0a_report.qmd).

### 6.2 Stage 0b — φ-convention sanity check

**The question.** You ran the simulation at `phi_sim = 89°` and compared against your `phi_exp = 0°` FTIR files. That mapping is empirical — does 89° actually beat its neighbours (0°, 1°, 90°)?

**Setup.** Locked NA = 39 from Stage 0a. Four $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ values, all compared against `12-3_30_0_*.CSV`.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage0b.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage0b.py) — 4 configs (with a resume run for an extra 89.999°), **12.6 min wall**.

**Result.**

| $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ | $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$($R_{\text{det}}$) | Pearson r | Notes |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 0° | — | — | **Singular matrix** — numerical degeneracy at perfect-symmetry azimuth |
| 1° | 254.78 | 0.835 | Conical mounting |
| **89°** | **224.89** | **0.932** | ← chosen |
| 89.999° | 597.36 | 0.935 | Near-90° branch (sudden jump) |
| 90° | 597.36 | 0.935 | Same degeneracy as 0° but flipped axis |

**Decision.** **$\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89° ↔ $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ = 0°** confirmed.

**One thing worth knowing.** `rcwa` throws **"Singular matrix"** at `phi_sim = 0°` exactly — the in-plane k-vector becomes parallel to a lattice reference axis and certain block matrices in the S-matrix construction lose rank. This is a known numerical degeneracy, not a bug in your setup. The workaround for any future need to "run at $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 0°" is to use 0.001° instead. Your decision to run at 89° (one degree off the 90° branch, not the 0° branch) sidesteps the degeneracy cleanly — **that was a deliberate, principled choice**, not arbitrary.

**Sanity check.** The $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ at ($\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89°, NA = 39) here is **224.89**, which is bit-identical to the (NA = 39) row from Stage 0a. The runs are consistent across stages with matching parameters. ✅

The detailed report: [`simulation/sweep/reports/stage0b_report.qmd`](simulation/sweep/reports/stage0b_report.qmd).

### 6.3 Stage 1 — Universal Tier-1 sweep

**The question.** Holding the per-sample geometry fixed at your AFM nominal (period = 12.9 µm, A = 1.5 µm → depth = 3.0 µm), find the universal triple `(t_oxide, β, oxide_dispersion)` that best fits the spectrum.

**Setup.** Locked NA = 39, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89° from Stage 0. Grid:

- `t_oxide ∈ {0, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.50, 0.90}` µm — 7 values
- `β ∈ {1°, 2°, 5°, 10°, 20°, 30°}` — 6 values
- `oxide_dispersion ∈ {HS_caliente, RS_frio}` — 2 values
- Sample SS_12-3, ($\theta$, $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$) = (30°, 0°), one condition only

Total: **84 configurations**.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage1.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage1.py) with `caffeinate -i ... --parallel 4 --resume`. **3 h 35 min wall.**

**Result — the top 5 configurations.**

| $t_{\text{oxide}}$ (µm) | $\beta$ (°) | oxide | $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ | RMSE | Pearson r |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **0.9** | **1, 2, 5** | **HS_caliente** | **138.83** | **0.118** | **0.972** ← chosen |
| 0.9 | 1, 2, 5 | RS_frio | 153.81 | 0.124 | 0.965 |
| 0.9 | 10 | HS_caliente | 157.68 | 0.126 | 0.958 |
| 0.9 | 10 | RS_frio | 172.22 | 0.131 | 0.951 |
| 0.5 | 1, 2, 5 | HS_caliente | 202.05 | 0.142 | 0.940 |

**Decision.**

```
t_oxide          = 0.90 µm
β                = 2°  (any of {1, 2, 5} — they are degenerate at this t_oxide)
oxide_dispersion = HS_caliente
χ²_red           = 138.83    Pearson r = 0.972
```

**An honest moment.** **This is the same configuration you arrived at empirically** in your AJUSTE PDF (page 10): $t_{\text{oxide}}$ = 0.9 µm, $\beta$ = 2°, HS film. Two independent paths — your empirical fit hand-tuned against the FTIR, and my objective minimisation of $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ across an 84-point grid — converged on the same answer. That is the kind of cross-validation the sweep was designed to provide.

**But: the safety rail tripped.** Best $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ = 138.83 is *much* bigger than 1. Per [`DISTANCE.md §6`](simulation/design/DISTANCE.md), this means **Stage 2 must not proceed** — proceeding would let `period` and `depth` absorb a structural error and give a falsely confident geometric fit.

**Where the residual is, in physical terms.**

- Pearson r = 0.972 → *shape* of `R_det(λ)` is already almost right.
- The remaining $\chi^{2}$ is dominated by **amplitude offset** (~10–15 pp uniform drop the simulation needs to make).
- The best $t_{\text{oxide}}$ is at the **edge of the explored range** (0.9 µm). The trend is still falling, so a *thicker* oxide would fit better — except this is your nominal placeholder and you have not directly measured it.
- The non-monotonic dip from `t_oxide = 0.3 → 0.5 → 0.9` ($\chi^{2}$: 225 → 202 → 139) suggests **interference structure** — a Fabry-Pérot-like cancellation in the oxide. That is physically meaningful, not a numerical artefact.

**Diagnosis from this stage.** The dominant error is **amplitude**, not feature alignment. The most likely culprit (per `ANALYSIS.md §4 / §6.3`) is the **Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ extinction-coefficient model** — it extrapolates the Al-Kuhaili sub-bandgap-tail fit 10× past its 0.3–2.5 µm range and contains no phonon physics. **Replacing the empirical $k(\lambda)$ with a literature $\varepsilon(\lambda)$ including the Reststrahlen band is the single largest upgrade available**, and that is exactly what should be tried next when you (or anyone) pick this up post-TFM.

The detailed report: [`simulation/sweep/reports/stage1_report.qmd`](simulation/sweep/reports/stage1_report.qmd).

### 6.4 The double-sinusoid follow-up

**The question.** Section 5 of your *Tratamiento* PDF shows the AFM mean profile has **broader peaks and sharper valleys** than a pure sinusoid — a non-sinusoidal asymmetry. Can a second-harmonic term `A₂ sin(2 k x + π/2)` reproduce that, and does it close any of the residual?

**Setup.** Locked Stage-1 best ($t_{\text{oxide}}$ = 0.9, $\beta$ = 2°, HS_caliente, NA = 39, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89°, period = 12.9, $A_1$ = 1.5, $\theta$ = 30°). Sweep `A₂ ∈ {0.10, 0.20, 0.30, 0.35}` µm at fixed `φ₂ = π/2`.

**Constraint.** The double-sin profile must keep its peak as a peak (not become a saddle). For `A₂ < A₁/4 = 0.375 µm` the local minimum stays a local minimum. The chosen range respects that bound.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/run_double_sin_test.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/run_double_sin_test.py) — 4 configs at 3 workers, **~14 min wall** total across two invocations.

**Result.**

| $A_2$ (µm) | $\varphi_2$ | $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ | RMSE | Pearson r | Δ$\chi^{2}$ vs $A_2$ = 0 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 0.00 (baseline) | — | 138.83 | 0.118 | 0.972 | — |
| 0.10 | $\pi$/2 | 126.75 | 0.113 | 0.978 | −12.1 |
| 0.20 | $\pi$/2 | 113.77 | 0.107 | 0.983 | −25.1 |
| 0.30 | $\pi$/2 | 104.18 | 0.102 | 0.983 | −34.6 |
| **0.35** | $\pi$/2 | **101.10** | **0.101** | 0.980 | **−37.7** |

**Decision.** **$A_2$ = 0.30 µm, $\varphi_2$ = $\pi$/2.** Going from $A_2$ = 0.30 to 0.35 buys only a few extra $\chi^{2}$ and starts hurting Pearson r — we are at the sweet spot. **The 2nd harmonic is real and worth carrying**, with a 25 % $\chi^{2}$ reduction over the pure sinusoid.

**One small bug worth flagging.** `run_double_sin_test.py` had a `--resume` bug: when re-invoked, the final CSV write was unconditional and overwrote `results.csv` with just the new rows, losing the older ones. The `traces/` directory was untouched so I rebuilt the table by re-scoring the saved trace folders. The fix is to merge against the existing CSV before writing, the way `run_stage0a.py` and `run_stage0b.py` do. [Flagged in `RUN_LOG.md` lessons.](RUN_LOG.md)

The detailed report: [`simulation/sweep/reports/double_sin_test_report.qmd`](simulation/sweep/reports/double_sin_test_report.qmd).

### What is locked after Stage 1 + double-sin

```
NA           = 39                  (Stage 0a)
φ_sim        = 89°  ↔  φ_exp = 0°  (Stage 0b)
t_oxide      = 0.90 µm             (Stage 1)
β            = 2°                  (Stage 1, plateau-degenerate with 1°, 5°)
oxide_disp   = HS_caliente         (Stage 1)
A₂           = 0.30 µm             (double-sin test)
φ₂           = π/2 rad             (double-sin test)
```

Every one of these matches your own empirical work where you state values explicitly, and the ones you do not state ($A_2$, $\varphi_2$) are physically motivated by the AFM asymmetry you reported.

## 7. Phase 6 — (θ, φ) validation, and the wall the model hit

### The question
The locked configuration fits `(θ = 30°, φ_exp = 0°)` well. Does it generalise across the **full 15-condition matrix** — 3 incidence angles × 5 azimuths — that you measured on sample SS_12-3?

### Setup
Locked params from §6.4. Sweep:
- `θ ∈ {30°, 45°, 60°}` × `φ_exp ∈ {0°, 22.5°, 45°, 67.5°, 90°}` = 15 cells
- $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ mapping: `φ_sim = 90° − φ_exp`, with the 1° offset at the singularities ($\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ 0° → $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ 89°, $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ 90° → $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ 1°)

### Run
[`simulation/sweep/bin/run_validate_thetaphi.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/run_validate_thetaphi.py) — 15 cells, 4 workers, **40.7 min wall**.

### Result — the matrix

**$\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ across ($\theta$, $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$):**

| $\theta$ \ $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ | 0° | 22.5° | 45° | 67.5° | 90° | row mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **30°** | 104 | 83 | **76** | 89 | 87 | **88** |
| **45°** | 263 | 232 | 139 | 142 | 96 | **174** |
| **60°** | **1158** | 1071 | 568 | 423 | 603 | **765** |

**Aggregate:** sum 5132 · mean 342 · median 142 · **max/min ratio = 15.3 ×**

**Pearson r across ($\theta$, $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$):**

| $\theta$ \ $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ | 0° | 22.5° | 45° | 67.5° | 90° |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **30°** | 0.98 | 0.97 | 0.97 | 0.95 | 0.95 |
| **45°** | 0.99 | 0.96 | 0.95 | 0.94 | 0.93 |
| **60°** | 0.94 | 0.89 | 0.86 | 0.86 | 0.86 |

### Reading the matrix

- **The whole $\theta$ = 30° row is healthy.** $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ sits in 75–104 (1.4× ratio), Pearson r $\geq$ 0.95 everywhere. **The $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 90° − $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ mapping is vindicated by this row's uniformity** — the $\varphi$ axis is consistent across all five azimuths, which is exactly what you would expect if the mapping is right.
- **At $\theta$ = 45° the residual roughly doubles** (mean $\chi^{2}$ 88 → 174). Shape is still excellent (r $\geq$ 0.93). *Usable with caveats.*
- **At $\theta$ = 60° the simulation breaks down.** $\chi^{2}$ is 423–1158, ten times the $\theta$ = 30° baseline. Pearson r drops below 0.90 at most azimuths — the **shape itself misaligns**, not just the amplitude.

### What happens physically at (θ = 60°, φ = 0°)

| | At $\theta$ = 30° | At $\theta$ = 60° |
|---|---:|---:|
| sim ⟨$R_{\text{det}}$⟩ (3–25 µm mean) | 0.60 | 0.69 |
| **exp ⟨R⟩** | **0.54** | **0.37** |
| sim − exp gap | +0.06 | **+0.33** |

The simulation predicts the sample reflects **70 %** of incident light at $\theta$ = 60°. The experiment sees **37 %**. The "missing" 33 percentage points must be going somewhere — light is being lost from the specular direction in a way the simulation cannot represent.

For a smooth metal at grazing, Fresnel says R should *increase* with $\theta$. The simulation gets that right. The experimental data does the *opposite* — R *drops* by ~30 pp going from $\theta$ = 30° to $\theta$ = 60°. **That pattern is unphysical for an idealised periodic surface.** It is a real measurement of *something* the model has no channel for.

The detailed report: [`simulation/sweep/reports/validate_thetaphi_report.qmd`](simulation/sweep/reports/validate_thetaphi_report.qmd).

---

## 8. Phase 7 — Two structural diagnostics that ruled themselves out

Before concluding "this is a physics-model gap, not a bug", I tested the two obvious bug hypotheses.

### Diagnostic (A) — semi-infinite substrate

**Hypothesis.** The 200 µm SS slab terminated by vacuum might allow back-reflections that contaminate `R_det` at large $\theta$ (longer internal path). Implemented `SimConfig.semi_infinite_substrate: bool = False` flag — when True, drops the explicit 200 µm metal_layer and sets `transmission_layer = Layer(er=ε_SS(λ), ur=1.000022)`.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/test_semi_infinite.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/test_semi_infinite.py) — 2 cells ($\theta$ = 30° and $\theta$ = 60° at $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ = 0°), **6.1 min wall**.

**Result.**

| Cell | Baseline (finite slab) | Semi-infinite | Δ$\chi^{2}$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| ($\theta$ = 30°, $\varphi$ = 0°) | 104.18 | 104.18 | **0.00** |
| ($\theta$ = 60°, $\varphi$ = 0°) | 1157.65 | 1157.65 | **0.00** |

**Bit-identical at both cells, both metrics.** Reason: skin depth in our band is 50–200 nm; 200 µm of SS is already 3–4 orders of magnitude thicker, so light decays by $\geq$ e⁻²⁵⁰⁰ before reaching the back surface. The substrate is *already* optically semi-infinite. [`ANALYSIS.md §6.7`](ANALYSIS.md) was geometrically valid but physically irrelevant.

**(A) REJECTED.**

### Diagnostic (B) — NA convergence at θ = 60°

**Hypothesis.** NA = 39 was chosen at $\theta$ = 30° (Stage 0a). Larger $\theta$ generally demands more harmonics because more diffraction orders propagate closer to the sample plane. Maybe NA = 39 is undersized at grazing.

**Run.** [`simulation/sweep/bin/test_na_at_theta60.py`](simulation/sweep/bin/test_na_at_theta60.py) — NA $\in$ {39, 51, 75, 91} at the worst cell ($\theta$ = 60°, $\varphi$ = 0°). **47.2 min wall** (NA = 91 is the bottleneck).

**Result.**

| NA | $\chi^{2}_{\text{red}}$ | RMSE | Pearson r | Δ vs NA = 39 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **39** (baseline) | **1157.65** | 0.340 | 0.942 | — |
| 51 | 1179.19 | 0.343 | 0.945 | +1.9 % |
| 75 | 1201.21 | 0.347 | 0.947 | +3.8 % |
| 91 | 1210.09 | 0.348 | 0.947 | +4.5 % |

**$\chi^{2}$ goes the wrong way with NA.** Adding harmonics makes the fit *slightly worse*, not better. NA = 39 is fully converged at $\theta$ = 60°. The disagreement is **not numerical**.

**(B) REJECTED.**

### Combined verdict
Both "is it a bug?" suspects eliminated. The $\theta$-dependent failure is a **physics-modelling gap**, not a numerics or geometry-wrap-up bug.

---

## 9. Phase 8 — Domain of validity

The definitive write-up of this conclusion is in [`simulation/design/MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md`](simulation/design/MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md). Three classes of physical loss the current model has no channel to represent, in rough order of likely contribution:

### 9.1 Diffuse scattering from non-periodic surface roughness
Your AFM data (Section 4 of *Tratamiento*) shows the surface profile has a $\pm\sigma$ envelope around the mean periodic structure — height fluctuations beyond the sinusoid itself. RCWA on a *perfect* periodic profile has only two channels for incident energy: propagating diffraction orders (a discrete set determined by the grating equation) or absorption inside the discretised structure. **There is no mechanism for energy to leave in non-grating directions as diffuse scatter.** Real surface roughness scatters light into a continuum of directions, removing it from the specular order. At grazing incidence this fraction grows because the effective optical interaction with surface fluctuations rises with the path-length-to-feature-size ratio. The simulation over-predicts specular at all $\theta$, but the gap is invisible at $\theta$ = 30° and dominant at $\theta$ = 60°.

### 9.2 Geometry-amplified Cr₂O₃ absorption
At $\theta$ = 60°, the optical path through the 0.9 µm oxide is `t / cos(60°) = 1.8 µm` — **2× the path at $\theta$ = 30°**. The Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ $k(\lambda)$ we use is the sub-bandgap tail from Al-Kuhaili & Durrani 2007, **extrapolated 10× past its 0.3–2.5 µm fit range**. It contains **no phonon physics** (no Reststrahlen band — see [`ANALYSIS.md §4`](ANALYSIS.md)). If our $k(\lambda)$ underestimates the true absorption (almost certainly does, in the IR), that error is amplified by the path-length ratio at grazing.

### 9.3 Polarisation handling at grazing
We average `R_LX` and `R_LY` (Cartesian-x and Cartesian-y) to model an unpolarised source. At normal-ish incidence ($\theta$ = 30°) the difference between TE and TM reflectance is modest; the LX/LY average is a reasonable proxy for unpolarised. At grazing, TE and TM diverge sharply (Fresnel), and any imperfect mapping between (LX, LY) and (TE, TM) shows up as a $\theta$-dependent error. Probably a smaller effect than (9.1) and (9.2) but contributes.

### What none of these are
None is fixable by *parameter tuning*. They are gaps in *what the model represents*. Adding more parameters (period, depth, $\beta$, oxide thickness) cannot create the missing physical channels. This is why $\chi^{2}$ actually got *slightly worse* in Diagnostic (B): refining the harmonic basis just makes the (wrong) idealised model more accurate, which does not help.

### What this domain analysis buys us
- **A clean statement of where the model is trustworthy.** Sample SS_12-3, $\lambda$ $\in$ [3, 25] µm, $\theta$ $\leq$ 30° — Pearson r $\geq$ 0.95 across the full azimuth row, ~6 pp residual amplitude offset attributable to the oxide phonon model.
- **A clean statement of where it is not.** $\theta$ $\geq$ 45° marginal; $\theta$ $\geq$ 60° unusable. Document this as a *finding about the model*, not as a failure of the campaign.
- **A prioritised list of future research directions** ([`MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md §8.3`](simulation/design/MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md)): Lorentz-oscillator Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ phonon model (~2–5 days), Rayleigh-Rice scattering correction (~1–2 days), AFM-mean-profile substitution for the idealised sinusoid (~2–3 days). Each is a research project; none is required for the TFM result.

---

## 10. Where this leaves us (bottom line)

### The result, in one paragraph
**At $\theta$ = 30° on sample SS_12-3, $\lambda$ $\in$ [3, 25] µm**, the simulation reproduces your experimental FTIR with **Pearson r between 0.95 and 0.98 across the full azimuth row**, with a residual amplitude offset of about 6 percentage points that is attributable to the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ phonon model (a known extrapolation outside its fit range). The configuration that achieves this — `(NA = 39, t_oxide = 0.9 µm, β = 2°, HS_caliente, A₂ = 0.30 µm, φ₂ = π/2)` — **matches your independent empirical fit exactly** in every parameter you committed to in the AJUSTE PDF. Two independent methods, one answer.

### Stage 2 is the natural next step
Per-sample geometry refinement under the locked Tier-1 universals. **At $\theta$ = 30° only.** The plan is in [`simulation/design/SWEEP_PLAN.md`](simulation/design/SWEEP_PLAN.md) § "Stage 2 — per-sample Tier-2". I did not run it yet because the biggest leverage move remains the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ phonon model upgrade — once that lands, Stage 2 should re-baseline at a much lower $\chi^{2}$ and any geometry refinement would land at the *right* basin instead of fitting around the oxide error.

### What's locked, what's parked

```
Locked (do not change):
    NA           = 39                    (Stage 0a, reverified at θ = 60° in Diagnostic B)
    φ_sim        = 89° ↔ φ_exp = 0°      (Stage 0b)
    t_oxide      = 0.90 µm               (Stage 1; matches AJUSTE p.10)
    β            = 2°                    (Stage 1; matches AJUSTE p.11)
    oxide_disp   = HS_caliente           (Stage 1)
    A₂           = 0.30 µm               (double-sin test)
    φ₂           = π/2 rad               (double-sin test)
    domain       = θ ≤ 30°               (validate_thetaphi + Diagnostics A, B)

Parked (future research):
    Cr₂O₃ phonon-aware k(λ)              (highest-leverage upgrade)
    Rayleigh-Rice diffuse-scatter term   (would extend domain past θ = 30°)
    AFM-mean-profile substitution        (refines the surface shape further)
    Stage 2 (per-sample geometry)        (waiting on the phonon model)
    Stage 3 (generalisation to 5 others) (waiting on Stage 2)
```

## 11. How to run things — commands

### One-time setup

```bash
cd 20260508_ane_corujo_simulations
python3.12 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt          # rcwa, numpy, scipy, matplotlib, pandas, jupyter
```

Then drop my (your, really) patched `solver.py` and `harmonics.py` into the venv's `rcwa/` site-packages directory:

```bash
SP=$(python -c "import rcwa, os; print(os.path.dirname(rcwa.__file__))")
# copy the patched files extracted from 20260508_messages/ane-thread-archive-2026-05-08.md
# (they include theta_orders and get_detected_reflectance)
cp /path/to/patched/solver.py    "$SP/solver.py"
cp /path/to/patched/harmonics.py "$SP/harmonics.py"
```

### Run one simulation, exactly as you would have

```bash
cd simulation
quarto render exploratory/simulate.qmd
```

Reads parameters from a single dict at the top of the document, runs RCWA, writes the trace under `simulation/exploratory/runs/adhoc/`, opens the HTML report. This is your `test8.qmd` made parameterisable.

### Compare a simulation against experiment

```bash
quarto render simulation/exploratory/compare.qmd
```

No RCWA solve — pure visualisation. Edit the document to point at any `AVG_*.csv` you want to plot against the FTIR triple.

### Run an entire sweep stage in batch

```bash
caffeinate -i python simulation/sweep/bin/run_stage1.py --parallel 4 --resume
```

`--resume` is essential — every script is restartable by reading existing `results.csv` and skipping configs whose trace already exists. `caffeinate -i` keeps the laptop awake on macOS. Stage 1 is 3.5 hours on this machine.

### Render a sweep report

```bash
quarto render simulation/sweep/reports/stage1_report.qmd
```

Loads `simulation/sweep/runs/stage1_universals/results.csv` and renders the analysis. Render time is seconds, no RCWA.

## 13. What I changed in your code, and what I did not touch

### Untouched — bit-for-bit
- Every file in [`20260508_messages/`](20260508_messages/) is exactly as you sent it.
- Every parameter in your `test8.qmd §5` cell that you committed to (period, $A_1$, NA, $\beta$, $t_{\text{oxide}}$, oxide_dispersion, slices, polarisations, $\theta$, $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$) has the same numerical value in the active `sweep_runner.py`, and the scripts that arrived at those values via the sweep land on your numbers.
- The Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ dispersion CSVs ([`data/materials/Cr2O3_*.csv`](data/materials/)) are frozen copies of `calientes_cromo.csv` / `indices_cromo.csv` — same numbers, more legible filenames.
- Your `solver.py` and `harmonics.py` patches to `rcwa` are unchanged. The active pipeline depends on them — `Solver.get_detected_reflectance(β)` and `Solver.theta_orders` are your additions, and they are load-bearing.

### Changed — structural, not physical
- **The `test8` simulation cell is now a function.** `sweep_runner.solve_one(cfg)` takes a `SimConfig` and returns a DataFrame; the cell's contents are unchanged inside.
- **The `R_det` filtering is identical.** `R_det(β) = Σ R_m` for orders with `|θ_m − θ_specular| ≤ β/2` — verbatim from your `_rt_quantities` patch.
- **The polarisation averaging is identical.** `R = (R_LX + R_LY) / 2`, the same Cartesian basis you used.
- **Filenames and paths.** Two cosmetic but real changes:
  - The SS data file's underlying values are complex permittivity, not `n, k`. I have not renamed the column headers because the symlink [`data/materials/SS_permittivity.csv`](data/materials/SS_permittivity.csv) points back at `SS_letter (1).csv` and the code reads the columns correctly regardless of the labels. The `README.md` next to the materials data calls this out explicitly.
  - All paths are relative or environment-driven. No Windows paths in the active code; your `Representacion.ipynb` hard-coded `r'C:\Users\usuario\Desktop\TFM\…'` would not run on macOS.
- **Two added knobs as opt-in switches**, both default-off so the active code is bit-identical to your pipeline:
  - `SimConfig.semi_infinite_substrate: bool = False` — when True, drops the 200 µm SS slab and sets the transmission half-space to SS. Tested and proven physically irrelevant (Diagnostic A), kept as a switch in case future work needs it.
  - `SimConfig.A2_um: float = 0.0` and `SimConfig.phi2_rad: float = 0.0` — second-harmonic amplitude and phase. Default (0, 0) recovers your pure sinusoid exactly.

### Documented but **not** patched (HIGH severity, on purpose)
- **The oxide-skin geometry** — vertical band vs normal-to-surface ([`ANALYSIS.md §6.4`](ANALYSIS.md)). I documented it but did not patch it: at our slopes ($\leq$ 36°) the maximum effect is ~25 % path-length error on the slopes, and we have higher-leverage problems first (the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ phonon model).
- **The Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ $k(\lambda)$ extrapolation** ([`ANALYSIS.md §4 / §6.3`](ANALYSIS.md)). This is the parked future-research item that, once fixed, should drop $\chi^{2}$ substantially. I did not implement a Lorentz-oscillator replacement because it is a 2–5 day research project in its own right, not a one-evening patch.

## 14. Open questions for you

These are the things I would ask you over coffee, in order:

1. **What is the actual FTIR detector half-angle?** $\beta$ = 2° is my Stage-1 winner, $\beta$ = 1° / 2° / 5° are degenerate — that whole plateau means "narrow cone, only the specular order survives". If you happen to know the spec sheet number, it would either confirm or sharpen this. ([`DISTANCE.md §3`](simulation/design/DISTANCE.md) flags this as the one external question that closes the loop on $\beta$.)

2. **Have you ever directly measured the Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ overlayer thickness on one of these samples?** XPS depth profile, ellipsometry, profilometry, anything. My winning $t_{\text{oxide}}$ = 0.9 µm is at the *edge* of the grid I swept, and the $\chi^{2}$-vs-$t_{\text{oxide}}$ curve was still falling — the true minimum is plausibly thicker than 0.9 µm. Two paragraphs of measured evidence would replace several days of additional sweeping.

3. **Cold dispersion parameters.** You shipped `indices_cromo.csv` for the RS films, but the `datos_cromo` cell only documents the HS coefficients (a₀ = 0.010, a₁ = −0.04121, a₂ = 0.041509, E₀ = 5.13 eV, $E_d$ = 19.2 eV). It would be helpful to have the RS coefficients committed next to those, so the CSVs can be regenerated from source when the model changes.

4. **The 89° vs 1° puzzle.** Stage 0b confirmed your $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 89° ↔ $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ = 0° empirically. But at the *other* end of the azimuth row ($\varphi_{\text{exp}}$ = 90°) I had to use $\varphi_{\text{sim}}$ = 1° to dodge the same singularity, and the matching is still good. Do you have an intuition (or a derivation) for why the rcwa azimuth convention sits at "90° − $\varphi_{\text{exp}}$"? It is the right answer but I would like to know *why* it is the right answer.

5. **Did your AFM data give per-sample $\sigma$ envelopes, or just a single trace?** Section 4 of *Tratamiento* shows the $\pm\sigma$ envelope is real for SS_12-3 and is wider in valleys than at peaks. If you have that for the other five samples, a Rayleigh-Rice scattering correction with a per-sample $\sigma$_h fit (one of the parked research items) becomes immediately tractable.

6. **Are there published Cr$_{2}$O$_{3}$ $\varepsilon(\lambda)$ tables in the mid-IR you trust?** If so, the highest-leverage upgrade (the phonon-aware k model) goes from a 5-day project to a few hours of editing.

## 15. A word about the documents themselves

Three documents in this repo, beyond this guide, are written specifically to be self-contained references rather than scratch notes:

- **[`ANALYSIS.md`](ANALYSIS.md)** — what your code does, where the physics is solid, where it is fragile. Written before any sweep was run. The §6 issues catalogue is the most useful single page if you ever decide to extend the model.
- **[`simulation/design/DISTANCE.md`](simulation/design/DISTANCE.md)** — the formal distance metric and the principled tiering of configuration space. The doctrine that prevents the sweep from misleading us.
- **[`simulation/design/MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md`](simulation/design/MODEL_DOMAIN_OF_VALIDITY.md)** — where the model works, where it breaks, and what physical channels are missing. The document I would attach to any future paper using this code.

The other two:

- **[`DESIGN_LOG.md`](DESIGN_LOG.md)** — verbatim record of the design discussions that produced `DISTANCE.md` and `SWEEP_PLAN.md`. Long. Useful if you ever wonder "why did they decide to factor it this way, not that way" — the answers are in here.
- **[`RUN_LOG.md`](RUN_LOG.md)** — one section per simulation run. Command, wall time, decision, lessons learned. The factual record.
